claims.text: Classical molecular dynamics can be used to investigate the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles varies measurably with particle size.
The size-dependent response includes changes in the onset of surface reconstruction, atomic diffusion, and phase stability.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are randomly mixed.
Particle diameters from approximately 2 to 10 nm are an appropriate range for this study.
Elevated-temperature ramps can be applied in molecular dynamics simulations to compare nanoparticle sizes.
Embedded-atom-method potentials have been validated for relevant transition-metal high-entropy alloys.
Thermal cycling produces lattice distortions and diffusion-driven atomic rearrangements.
The thermally induced atomic rearrangements are size dependent.
High configurational entropy, local elemental interactions, and atomic diffusion jointly determine structural rearrangement and surface segregation.
Nanoparticle size determines the extent of structural rearrangement, surface segregation, and solid-solution phase retention.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit surface reconstruction at lower temperatures than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles show greater temperature-driven elemental redistribution than larger particles.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo delayed transitions and less compositional segregation.
Multicomponent-alloy molecular dynamics studies have found strong chemical clustering over a broad temperature range.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can undergo substantial temperature-dependent structural and chemical evolution driven by diffusion.
Specific thermal-response data for FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles remain limited.
Predictions may change with composition, interatomic potential, or heating rate.
Exact transition-size thresholds and high-temperature composition profiles depend on force-field accuracy.
The predicted size dependence can be falsified if in situ heating experiments find no correlation between particle size and the onset temperature of structural changes.
